utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you following the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Wubben, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben. Also good morning to the learned friends from the Defence. I am here together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers, and later on this morning -- or actually imminent to arrive is Ms. Joanne Richardson also included in the team. And our acting case manager Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Oric. With us this morning are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Wubben, or Mr. Jones. Just the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday we filed a request for receiving the original Prosecution exhibit. I referred to it, and this morning Defence counsel already expressed to me her opinion about it and she might convey that to this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who is going to address that? We are talking of P561, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not object to having that document handed over for an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I am not suggesting now to proceed with an oral decision because I haven't seen the motion as yet, so I would rather prefer to see it in its entirety and then, if necessary, come back to you in the break with an oral decision. But I wouldn't like to hasten and grant the motion without seeing it first. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there are a couple of other preliminaries, Your Honour. First for the record, we want to object to the use of the exhibits on the Prosecution exhibit list. I won't name all of them, but it's roughly between P3 and P608 for the following reason. We've challenged the authenticity as far as I know of all of those documents. They haven't been shown to -- in our submission, to Defence witnesses who would have been in a position to comment on their contents, which is -- again, it's an issue of Rule 90(H)(ii) which we've raised. Instead we anticipate that the Prosecution will seek to authenticate these documents by showing them to this witness who was only in Srebrenica in March 1993 and who will not be familiar with the documents or with any of the events described, and that is something which we consider is improper. There's another aspect of that which is that since we challenge the authenticity of these documents, we're aware that Your Honour's indication that obviously you don't want us to indicate in front of the witness that we object to authenticity. But equally, I submit, that that has to go both ways and that it shouldn't be suggested either that the documents are authentic to the witness. For example, being -- presenting a witness with a document and saying, Does that change your mind about such-and-such. It would have to be a question along the lines of, If what is described in here is correct then would that change your mind. Otherwise the witness is under the impression that we accept authenticity. And so that's -- that's an auxiliary matter, an auxiliary matter, to the general objection. And I do reserve the right during cross-examination to object that if the witness isn't asked with each document, Are you familiar with the contents, are you familiar with Voljavica or the events described in the document, and the question is hypothetical, if what is in this document, would such-and-such be the case, then I certainly object to that because this witness isn't here to answer hypothetical questions but to answer questions based on his knowledge. And that leads to a third aspect of all of this, which is that if the Prosecution do present each one of these documents and put a hypothetical question to the witness along the lines of if what is here, described here is true, then would as such-and-such be the case. Then I'm going to have to in re-examination go through every single document and ask the witness, Are you familiar with this document; can you see whether it was sent or received; do you know these places; are you able to tell us anything about the document. And I'll certainly do that, but I just submit that it's just better to be clear beforehand whether it's a useful exercise for this witness to see these documents and then and we might save an hour and a half or two hours of cross-examination and re-examination. There are two other preliminaries which I may as well mention -- mention now. They are not related to my first point. One is a matter of timing. I've been I think so far two hours and 14 minutes with this witness. I anticipate I can finish in about 20 minutes or half an hour. I know that the witness is keen to finish today because he has travel plans, and in fact equally the witness for tomorrow would also -- has family commitments, which would make it best if he could also travel by the end of business tomorrow. So I just mention that so that Your Honours are aware that that's a schedule which would certainly suit the witnesses and, I imagine, the Court. If I'm finished in half an hour, then that means I would have been two hours and 45 minutes, and unless the Prosecution is going to be longer than I was in examination-in-chief, we should be able to finish with him today. And then the other matter is yesterday there was this question of replacing exhibits with other exhibits. I can say that having reviewed the matter we don't object for P600, which as we recall the second page of the document was shown by Ms. Richardson in court, and that's not something we have a problem with. Or P607, which is just a question of the English translation. We do object for P605, however. At the time you may recall Ms. Richardson referred to judicial notice, and we objected to -- in fact, there was submission regarding that document. In fact, the witness didn't see the page which was being relied on, which was referring to a specific person. This is the hearing of the 29th of November, 2005. We can look at it all later. But in our submission if he had seen that page he would have seen the date of birth of this person and other details, and he could have said, Well, that's not true or that's false. He should have had a right to comment on this page rather than it being entered later, and so we say that that -- that's -- if the Prosecution wish to tender that page, then they'll have to do it through another witness. Those -- that's our preliminaries, unless I can assist you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Sellers, do you want to comment on -- first of all, the -- let me clear this, because you said, at least according to the transcript, the documents between P603 and P608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, P3, not 603. Okay. Then the transcript needs to be corrected. All right? So you contest all those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I didn't go through one by one because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. But I take it that you contest all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Including the two on the cert pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe it's on the record already that we object to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's clear. Ms. Sellers, you've heard the submission of Mr. Jones with regard to how you should or shouldn't make use of these documents. Do you agree with his submission or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be very willing to be amenable to the Defence, but I don't think I'll be able to agree with his arguments as set forth: I think that Defence counsel is certainly aware that the Prosecution knows that they've objected to these documents, and I'm happy that at least it was not raised in front of the witness. This witness will not be asked to authenticate signatures of this document. This witness will not be asked to go beyond, as a matter of fact, the capacities from which the Defence have called him. The Defence have called him on a matter which goes to tactics, which goes to military strategy, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In conclusion to this argument, I would strenuously object that the Prosecution is not allowed to put questions to this witness when these documents that relate to the very germane matters for which he was called. Now, if the Defence chooses to re-direct in a lengthy matter, I think that's a matter for the Defence and Your Honours. Your Honour, I do have one other matter I would like to -- two other matters I would like to bring up while I'm on my feet. And that is that we do have a new exhibit that we would like to give to the Defence prior to their starting today. And it's an exhibit of -- for this witness. It's called, "Tactics, Technicals, and Procedures of Combat." I believe that the Defence brought this up in the direct examination of the witness. We were able to secure copies. It appears that this witness is a co-author, if I look at the transcript correctly. I wanted to hand this over to the Defence before they start their examination today. And Your Honours will see from the document that it appears that the witness has testified in line with some of the pages directly in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see it as well. In the meantime, please hand a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: While that's being done, Your Honour, I would also like to hand up the revised translation of P80. This was discussed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just clarify one matter, and I trust the Prosecution isn't intending to use this as any part of their cross-examination. It's not on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's for this reason that I -- we didn't want to bring it up. I would like to use it for cross-examination. That's why I wanted to bring that up to both the Defence, to the Trial Chamber now before the witness has walked in. And as I stated, the Defence has made reference to this -- this manual in their direct examination as part of the knowledge of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I address you on this, Your Honour. In fact, we have a copy of this document. I didn't deal with this -- the contents of this document in examination-in-chief for the reason that actually to use these documents requires clearance from the United States government. They can't simply be tendered and used in that manner. And if the Prosecution wishes to tender it, then they'll have to seek authorisation from the United States government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, not only you. Once you have mentioned -- you've raised this matter up, we'll have to clear it up with the representatives of the embassy here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will certainly raise that with them if that's what the Defence's position is. We did not receive this document in that matter. If you'll notice, it does not have an ERN number nor a restricted ERN number. If we do not have such clearance, I certainly wouldn't want to violate anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. No, no. But I will not even --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We will refer to contents, as I believe the Defence has on direct, as opposed to the document, but that's something that we could take care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this publication or document readily available? Say, if I wanted to search for this in the public domain, either through -- on the Internet or -- would I be able to obtain it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we received it in such a manner. But I would like to clarify that, importantly, because as you can see, it is not part of our evidentiary bank. Let me clarify that before we would use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just -- to further matters, Your Honour, just to perhaps assist the Court. Not only did we have this document but we did discuss this with the US government, and we even sent a request to be authorised to use it, and we've received that authorisation, but we've decided -- and it was a calculation based on how much time we had not to get into it. That's an authorisation which we have. The Prosecution, as I understand it, would have to seek their own authorisation. The second matter is I'm wondering when the Prosecution received this because there's exculpatory material in this, I can assure you, and why wasn't this disclosed to us in time rather than when we already started examining the witness in chief rather than -- and so we could actually proof him with it if we didn't have it. We do have it. But I can't understand whether the Prosecution are claiming they received this yesterday. If they received it before then, then I would ask why that hasn't been disclosed to us in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the past two days that we've gone through this document. On its face it speaks in generalities. If there's exculpatory material, we certainly would like the Defence to look at it now. But in our reviewing of this document, there's material that speaks in generalities about the areas of Srebrenica and not specifically about the accused nor about this case. Now, if it's been interpreted as being 68 material, I think there's only one place that I see that there might be a tendency toward it. But, Your Honours, I think the point more importantly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it necessary to have -- to make specific use of this with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't you refer to parts of it without showing the document itself to the witness and ask questions on whatever part from this document you would like him to testify upon? Because -- for example -- I mean, I don't know. Forces for attacking from the rear or fundamental tactics, if you want to deal with this, can't you put a proposition to the witness based on what you have here without actually showing him the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I certainly can do that. If that would facilitate matters more so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I -- sorry. That is what I understand the Defence did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That is what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why don't you do the same thing and avoid the entire discussion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will save us having to ask for permission from the two US representatives who could be extra cautious and say we have to go back to the State Department first and seek clearance from there. I don't know, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an approach I could take.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry, but this is terribly important. Firstly, if there's any possibility that the Prosecution are going to use this in cross-examination, then I will -- then I don't want to stop my examination-in-chief until I know whether I'm going to be able to use this document. If the Prosecution are going to use it in cross-examination, then I will certainly use it in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we need to clear that up first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't finished your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was going to finish in 20 minutes but I'll have to wait until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you haven't finished, in other words. You can use this document if you want to, especially since you've had clearance from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not my intention to. I want to see if the Prosecution will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, they won't be using this document, as I take it. They will be using it indirectly by making reference to it, without indicating to the witness that they are referring to a particular document, which is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And may I -- and for the second matter which is -- absolutely -- I find staggering is that the Prosecution mentioned receiving this a couple of days ago. I don't know if that was when they had their interview with our witness on Friday. But this, Your Honour, perhaps we can go into private session, but I can refer to matters which are clearly exculpatory, referring to no trained military leaders, the village chiefs became local commanders. This is clearly an exculpatory matter. The fact that this was not disclosed to us by the Prosecution until now is another Rule 68 violation. There is absolutely -- and Your Honours will see, there is no question that there is a lot of Rule 68 material here concerning what sort of potential for command and control existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the ground clear now, in military terms, so that we can bring in Lieutenant Colonel Dudley?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to clarify then from Your Honour's and the Trial Chamber's instructions is that instead of tendering this, I can refer to some of the contents in terms of my questioning. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Listen, I'm not taking decisions for you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision belongs to you. Equally it belongs to Mr. Jones. If he wants to make use of this document between now and when he ends his examination-in-chief, he is free to do so. I mean, I cannot restrict him. Him or you. But please do take into consideration that while Mr. Jones has already had clearance from the US government, you haven't. So basically, if you try to make use of this, if Mr. Jones hasn't made use of it and brought it into the records of the case as an exhibit, then we will have problems. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: An additional matter with a view to the preliminaries by Mr. Jones was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was the scheduling of the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There was expressed a kind of wish or request, I don't know, to end by close of business tomorrow. Can we discuss that after finalising this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would suggest that you discuss it amongst yourselves first. Because you can anticipate that we are not going to tell you, yes, definitely, we will finish tomorrow or, no, he won't finish tomorrow. I mean, we'll see. Yes. It's nice to get some adrenaline running in the system at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, may I state that upon the entry in the courtroom of the witness, the two representatives of the US State Department and also of the US Embassy here in The Hague showed up. That's Mr. Clifton Johnson and Ms. Heather Schildge. Good morning to you and welcome back. Good morning to you, Lieutenant Colonel, welcome back. We're going to proceed and finish with the direct and then we will have the cross-examination. We're starting now, because again, once more, that's actually almost a daily recurrence. We had procedural problems to deal with and decide upon. Believe me, this is no easy job. Thank you. So good morning to you. Mr. Jones, please, you may proceed with your direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Jones: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning from me, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I wonder if we could start with the witness being shown D229, please. Defence Exhibit 229. Just for the record, this is HQ BH command, dated 20th March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was, again, a time when you were actually in the enclave. And I'll direct your attention to paragraph 8. It's under "assessment" on the second page. It says: "The Serb attack on the Srebrenica enclave continues unabated. Despite the recent success of General Morillon to get the relief convoy into Srebrenica, the Serbs seem intent to continue this offensive as part of a general aim to continue to capture areas which can be taken at little cost. Currently the Serbs are clearing up to four to five villages per day. They have received a lot of support from across the border in Serbia during this offensive. The Serbians have supported the BSA with artillery fire, aircraft bombers, and ammunition re-supply convoys, as well as having allowed the Serbs to stage from within Serbian borders to attack from the east and south of the enclave." Pausing there, I just want to ask whether you can confirm that that -- whether that was the situation or not when you were there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be a very accurate statement of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it goes on. I'm just going to look at a couple of more paragraphs. Paragraph 9: "This offensive is creating a refugee situation of huge proportions. The number of refugees in the Srebrenica enclave is assessed to be around 80.000. It is estimated that there are 20.000 refugees in Srebrenica alone and an additional 20.000 in Zepa. The condition of many of the refugees is very poor. There are an estimated 200 seriously wounded and an additional 100 less seriously wounded. A death rate of 20 persons per day is reported. The pending massive medevac to Tuzla or any other single location would create a severe problem because of overcrowding in a city hospital there." Again, if you can comment at all on the situation as described there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only change I would have is I think the estimate that I had personally was 70.000 in the pocket versus 80.000. But again we're quibbling over numbers. The situation was very bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now paragraph 10, I won't read in full, but in summary it's dealing with the anticipated situation of Srebrenica would fall and with the refugees fleeing to Zepa. And the next paragraph states: "If free passage with transport cannot be arranged for the refugees in the Srebrenica pocket within the next 7 to 14 days, indications are that the Serbs will carry out a genocidal cleansing of the entire enclave, resulting in the potential death of up to 80.000 human beings. In any case, there is little hope that current efforts to get the Serbs to halt their attack will be successful. They are unlikely to stop this offensive until the enclave is cleared, one way or another." And my question based on that is: Is it right that you in fact reported or made similar predictions about what would happen if Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I wasn't predicting genocide per se, but I was definitely saying it was not going to be a pretty picture when the Serbs moved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you could tell, were the people in Srebrenica aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Again, I made a comment the other day that they appeared not to be much smarter than their animals that they owned. What I meant by that is that they were very desperate people and they were at the -- below what I call basic human needs level, and they were vying just for basic survival. And therefore they were killing, robbing, stealing, doing everything that they could just to survive, and that had reduced them almost to the level of animals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I think I'm moving to a different area now. Were you present when a Serb was released from Srebrenica and sent to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I believe that date was the 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember what time of day?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning and at approximately 10.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where had you spent the previous night?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had spent the previous night out on a drop zone watching a delivery of supplies, and I had come back, got a couple of hours sleep, and I was up talking to some guards and they needed help with the stretcher gear, and I volunteered to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "guards," are these Bosnians or internationals or who were they?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the Canadians who were guarding in front of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went south along the main road, and then there is a grocery store where the road forms a Y, and we headed off to the right side of that road and up the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you travelling in?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were travelling in the M-113, the Canadian M-113.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an APC?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did any other APCs travel with you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the only one that was in the pocket at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Morillon in the APC with you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his ADC with him in the -- with you in the APC?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Major Tucker?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I meant the Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about Major Tucker?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Tucker was in the APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where General Morillon and his body-guard went or where they were at that time?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an assumption, but because Major Tucker was up picking up the prisoner, I am assuming that he was down at the Bratunac bridge working with the Serbs to finalise the actual exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your assumption is that at this time General Morillon and his body-guard were at Bratunac, but you're not sure. It's simply that he wasn't with you in the APC?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And since that was the major action of the day, I would assume that's where he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you arrive at a location where the Serb was picked up?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's call that the pick-up location. Again, sorry, it may seem obvious, but to make this clear. Was General Morillon at the pick-up location?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was his body-guard?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do at that location?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dismounted from the armoured personnel carrier. We carried out the stretcher. At the exact same time, the Serb prisoner was being brought down the hill. We laid him on the stretcher and we picked him up and put him into the armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was anyone filming this scene?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tony Birtley was filming the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went past the PTT building down to a bridge south of Srebrenica, not as far as Bratunac but about halfway down. There weren't a whole lot of buildings around the area, and I remember a Serb defensive line on the far end of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the Serb then handed over to the Serbs in that location?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And around what time was that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I'm going to guess between 11.30 and 12.00 noon. It was definitely before 12.00 noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that handover location, did you see General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his body-guard?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would say he was there also because they were joined at the hip at all occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said how Tony Birtley was filming this scene. Did he continue to film the APC or did he stop before then?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Tony Birtley being at the bridge. I believe he got off before we left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you think of any reason why he did that?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither he nor I were very popular with the Serbs at that time, and I don't think he wanted to expose himself to being physically extracted from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the APC going from the pick-up location to the handover location, were you seated in the APC?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. And I believe I was at the front of the APC, close to the prisoner's head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were you near him?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was right next to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you got the Serb to the -- the Serb side, when he was handed over, what did the people there do?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They immediately crowded around him and started asking him questions. One of the officers chased them off. They carried him across the bridge and loaded him, I believe, onto another ambulance and he was gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then was that the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that was basically the end of the matter. We stood around and talked a little bit more. I had a discussion with a Serb officer about air-drops on their side of the enclave, outside the enclave, and then we loaded up and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now we have photographs to distribute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while that's being handed out, at the pick-up location, do you recall any mention of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone pointed out to you as Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- no, and I would have remembered it. One of the key things I remember is there were very few people around. Most of them were directly involved in picking up the prisoner, but I wouldn't say I saw any key players from the Bosnian side at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at that photograph, if it can be placed on the ELMO, I'm afraid it's a bit blurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pick out and identify of the people in that picture? Now first of all -- first of all, do you recognise this picture and what it shows?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the prisoner pick-up point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify anyone in that picture?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Staff Sergeant Morrison who was the NCO in charge of the Canadian group. This is the prisoner being helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's give this document an exhibit number to start with, and then we go through it in a correct manner. This will become Defence Exhibit D9?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 997. So can you go through this again slowly, sir? The gentleman we see on the left with the cap, you're pointing at that person, who is that person according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Staff Sergeant Morrison. He was the NCO in charge of the Canadian team that was with us in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And to his right there is a man with a cap and a jacket. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are pointing that person. You don't know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. In between there is a semi-reclined figure. Is that the prisoner that was eventually exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could we say "stooping figure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stooping figure. All right. Is it important for you to identify any of the others? There I see two persons with a cap and a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, if the colonel could identify the person he was just pointing to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the one with the helmet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the Canadian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the one with the cap, extreme right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is yourself. All right. There is another person with a cap in the foreground just in front of where you are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Major Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is Major Tucker. And at the -- at your -- at the back behind you, there is -- behind you, there is a person who seems to be wearing a kind of a camouflage uniform, et cetera. Can you identify that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I do not know who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Does that cover everyone that you needed to identify in this photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall roughly where this location was?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Inside Srebrenica. I can generally point to the general area. It was a fancy building with very nice stone work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to show a picture now and it's from C2. That should appear on the monitor. Now, would that -- would the building on the right -- is that the location?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Can I make a quick comparison between the two photographs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the original photograph that shows the prisoner exchange, you will see the rock wall at the base of both photographs, you will see the horizontal bar in both photographs. You will see the same type of stone work above, and you will also see that the bars on the windows and the spacing is almost exactly the same. That was the only building like that in Srebrenica that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, on this occasion, you told us how you were in the APC - and we've finished with that photograph exhibit - that you were near this detainee. At that time, at the pick-up, did you also get close to him?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was very close to him. I was sitting, again, close to his head. One of my key remembrances is that he reeked. He smelled very badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any signs that this Serb had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see any physical signs that he had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any signs of bruising or bleeding on his face?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no signs of either bruising or bleeding on his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any bandages on his face?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no bandages on his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a second photograph to distribute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us whether you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the prisoner that we were exchanging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where this is shot from?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is shot inside the M-113, and the hatch to the M-113 was open, so therefore he's protecting his eyes because he came out of a dark room. Covering his eyes, trying to protect them a little bit from the sunlight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record, this photo that the witness is being shown, referring to, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us and we can see from this picture that there was no bandages and no signs of bruising or blood or beating on his face?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roger. I gave the prisoner several good looks, again just being a military observer. I would like to point out a few things that I noticed and remember to this day. First, you'll notice that his hands are very dirty. He obviously had not been washed. You notice the length of his hair. He had been confined for I suspect at least two months since it had become rather long and shaggy. I was amazed that He didn't have much of a beard. He appears to have just a light goatee. His eyes are very shrunken, which shows to me that he's malnourished. And again his clothes were dirty but intact. He had a complete set of clothing on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were in Srebrenica, were there other people, Muslims, who were in such a state?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The entire population was starving at this time, and most of them were very malnourished, and so I would say this is a very typical appearance of a lot of people inside Srebrenica. They could walk a little better than he could, but they were still in very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court would indulge me, I need a five-minute break in order to verify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Ms. Sellers. We will have a five-minute break. I suggest that everyone stays in the proximity of the courtroom. We will leave the courtroom for five minutes and we'll be back in five minutes' time. --- Break taken at 8.44 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ready? Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for giving me the five-minute break, which became a ten-minute break. I would like to put on the record that during that break the Prosecution availed themselves of the opportunity to speak to the United States government in relationship to the document that had been raised earlier in this session. And our question to the United States government was precisely in response to what the Defence had raised in terms of any Rule 68 material that might be contained within that document, and we've asked for permission from the US government: Could we release the document to the Defence counsel, in light of any Rule 68 material that we might feel is in the document. And I have been informed by the representatives that that will be possible, unless the Defence at this time states that they already have the document or if there's any other arrangements. If not, then we'll proceed in that fashion to make sure that they do have the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to comment on that, Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A bit more than we've received this already. I'm not sure -- is this post-talk that the Prosecution has received authorisation to release this to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, we have. In light of your concerns, and in light of our having the document more recently, we wanted to make sure that the Defence would be in possession of any Rule 68 material, and that's why we wanted to make the request forthwith. Not ad hoc, but expeditious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can close this incident here and proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the understanding that we will proceed unless the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not to concern ourselves -- we are not concerned with that. I mean -- yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Unless I've completely misunderstood. This has been disclosed to us, the Prosecution is conceding that it's Rule 68 material. That's fine. I don't understand Ms. Sellers to be saying that she's going to use this. We have an agreement on that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think that's the case. Ms. Sellers is concerned, as I take it, that the Prosecution will not be exposed at later -- any later point in time in not having disclosed a document containing Rule 68 material according to you and also according to her. And the problem that stood in the way after that you raised the matter was that, strictly speaking, the Prosecution did not yet have clearance from the US government. Now they have clearance or the prospect of clearance from the US government, and they are informing the Trial Chamber that they will be disclosing the document in compliance with the Rule 68 requirements. That's how I understood it. If I understood it wrongly, please correct me. It will not be the first and I promise you it will not be the last time I have misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have understood it quite correctly. And there is another slight technicality. I would have to ask the Defence. I believe that we gave them copies of the materials that we were going to use for our examination, and we will disclose this properly with a receipt. And so those materials that we have given you are basically not at this point disclosed to you. So let's not have any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another thing before you proceed with your cross-examination. Mr. Jones, what's the source of these two photos?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I prefer not to give evidence about that. It could be dealt with with the subsequent witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examined by Ms. Sellers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. As you know, I'm with the Prosecution. I'm going to be asking questions that pertain to many of the things that you've testified with on direct examination. If you do not understand my question, please ask me to repeat it or rephrase it. And certainly if you do not know of information that I'm trying to solicit, a simple yes or no will certainly suffice. If you would like to explain more fully to the Trial Chamber, just inform me. I would like to ask you again to just confirm that you were in Srebrenica in the enclave from March 20 -- from March 11th until March 28th. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you came to Srebrenica, you were, in essence, assigned or working with two persons, one named Zele and one named Senad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the two individuals that came forward and were able to -- initially they were my watchers, and then they became my interpreters and assistants once they were convinced that I was doing good for them and not bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the stage in which they were your watchers, would you please tell the Trial Chamber how they watched you.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I convinced the local authorities that I needed to make some communication shots in order to coordinate the air-drops. That got me out of the PTT building, and we moved to the south of Srebrenica to get to the top of a hill to do an initial TacSat shot. Senad was the first one to go with me, and he was right next to me and listening to every word that I said on the tactical satellite system. He was making sure that I was not putting out any information that he did not approve of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is Senad the one who was dressed in military garb, if I can state as much?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a beret and camouflage and carry a weapon, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be specifically, he wore a green beret. He had camouflage jacket and pants and a form of combat boots. He wore either a North Korean or Chinese protective vest which had his AK banana clips in front of it, and he carried either a North Korean or a Chinese Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the other person, Zele, could you tell us how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was usually dressed informally. Occasionally I saw him in police garb, and the key thing that was always noticeable about him was he had one arm. He had lost his arm earlier in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who sent Senad and Zele to you to be your watchers at this point?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Senad told me that he had been sent by Naser. However, I was never able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Naser," did you take that to mean Naser Oric or did you take that to mean another Naser?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took that to mean the military commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Senad and Zele first came to you, isn't it true that they threatened to kill you if certain rules or regulations weren't followed?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were there to assist me, but they indicated -- particularly Senad indicated that he was also there to kill me if I got out of hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why he would kill you if you came to Srebrenica to help?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the biggest concern was that they did not know who I was. I showed up as a professional military officer from the United States, and they weren't quite sure of exactly what I was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your point of view, is that the reason that you say that you were watched, that your communications were listened to?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were very concerned about what I was putting out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also concerned about where you went in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within the town itself and also in the outside pocket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever prohibited from going to certain locations or into certain buildings because of them?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested to go to certain locations, particularly to meet with the local military commander, who was stated to be Naser. And I was refused access to him on several -- you know, I was never allowed to see him or meet with him or the other military authorities inside Srebrenica. As far as freedom of access, once the first week had passed, I was out walking at night even without any hindrance to my ability to get around. It was just that first week that they were closely following me and watching my actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you somehow gain their confidence?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The key way I gained their confidence was being able to deliver air-drops at the place and point of times I said supplies were going to come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you delivered air-drops and were able to gain their confidence, then were you allowed to meet Naser?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever given a reasonable explanation from your point of view of why you could not meet Naser?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that first, okay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested to meet him. I never did meet him. I understand afterwards that he was in the general vicinity, but I was never, that I remember, introduced to him. And therefore, I would have to say -- I don't know whether he was just unavailable or just unwilling to meet with me. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of either the unavailability or the unwillingness, you were never able to see him face-to-face or be introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Ms. Sellers, I'd like to know from the interpreters whether they are happy with -- no. I think you need to slow down, both of you, particularly in allowing a short interval of time between question and answer, because I take it that the interpreters are finding it a little bit difficult in catching up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Dudley, because we are both English speakers, we're -- I'm asking the question and we're answering and we're going back and forth, and for our interpreters it would be better if we took the breaks. Now, even though you were never introduced to Naser and therefore I assume didn't recognise him, are you -- were you under the impression that both Zele and Senad were in communication with Naser while they were your watchers?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever give you any information concerning Naser Oric while you were there?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask for any information concerning Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask for specific information on him or about him. The only reason I was interested in him is I considered him one of the key players in assisting me to accomplish my mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you gained their confidence, were you able to talk to them about some of the experiences that they had had during the war or things that had happened in Srebrenica or the enclave during the war?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to talk to them about any actions that they had participated or in or any actions that they knew about?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you in terms of the manner in which actions or attacks were carried out from the Muslim side in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have stated a lot of this information yesterday. Some of the specific things that they personally mentioned as far as their individual actions in the enclave was that they would go out on small raiding parties and they would attack viciously and quickly. They would take no prisoners because they had no way of taking care of them or escaping with them. And they would be short, violent, probing attacks to keep the Serbs off balance. And Senad particularly, I know at least once while I was in the enclave, took off on one of those activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you described that yesterday, you mentioned that these were types of raids?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from your experience as a military intelligence officer, the types of raids that you're describing, what types of forces would normally partake in actions such as those?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say light infantry/guerrilla type personnel, and the reason why is they travel light and quickly and usually in the dark. And they're able to surprise whoever they're going after and can quickly hit hard and withdraw before the enemy forces can respond effectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there be a typical time of day when raids such as that would be carried out?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely. You do them between 2.00 and 6.00 in the morning, when the enemy is the most tired and the visibility is the poorest. And you would strike them just before -- a technical term is "early morning nautical twilight." Just as you can barely see shadows, but not much more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also in those type of actions that you're describing, would those type of actions involve small units, combined units, or large units?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: These would be basically small units, usually between 20 and a hundred men, and I would say maximum of a hundred men because you're making too much noise as you're approaching the target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm using the word "units," I could say brigades or battalions, but when you're speaking about these types of actions, the guerrilla warfares, is the term "units" used descriptive or is it still within a military sense?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit can be used for any organisation of people under arms. You can call a unit anywhere from a battalion all the way down to a small squad without specifying total numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I object to that, that comment by Ms. Sellers, "I could say brigades or battalions," that wasn't any part of the question about the meaning of the word "units." And certainly we know what the witness -- the evidence he gave in terms of describing groups, that was the term which he used. So I would object to the comments about "I could say brigades or battalions." I don't see how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She was using those terms in context of guerrilla warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to follow up my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think -- I do understand of course your objection, but I also understand that she was not putting to the witness that she was actually dealing with brigades or battalions. Anyway, let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Dudley, now I would like to say in using terminology such as "brigades" or "battalions" with what you've described as guerrilla forces, would that have to be a specified number or would that be a term of art used in the military?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're dealing with either guerrilla or small militias or other non-professional military, "unit" would be an appropriate term, also group, "guerrilla group" would also be an appropriate term. But, again the sizes, the capabilities, varies tremendously in that type of an environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with units or guerrilla groups in that type of nature, you've mentioned that they frequently would not take prisoners. So would you mean prisoners of war during these raids or these actions?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm wondering what the relevance of this is. It doesn't relate to any count in the indictment that I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can imagine what the relevance is, but Ms. Sellers will tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our indictment certainly concerns actions where prisoners have been taken clearly in the indictment and clearly the last part of the direct examination of my learned friend concerned prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to get back to my last question, and that is: With units or guerrilla groups in that type of nature you mentioned that they frequently would not take prisoners, prisoners of war in these type of actions. I would like to ask you to explain why.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first off, when you are moving quickly in that environment you can't afford to drag along somebody that will slow you down, particularly when you are retrograding after the attack. The other one is that you have no place to hold him, and particularly if you're living hand to mouth yourselves, you don't want an extra mouth to have to feed or to take care of. The only reasons that you would take a prisoner in this situation is when there is a prisoner exchange and/or to gain military information from that prisoner, if you thought they possibly possessed it. Like if you've captured a higher-ranking officer, by chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "a prisoner exchange," could I take that to mean to exchange your prisoners for prisoners from the other side that could be your own fighting forces?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roger. One of the key things was morale of small groups particularly in this type of an environment is getting back your dead wounded and/or live personnel. And then you will of course take prisoners in order to exchange that. Give somebody to the enemy so you can get your own back. Very common practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there also be any practices of the times that you would exchange prisoners that you captured probably for valuable goods, whether it be food or whether it be weapons or ammunitions?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On occasion if the enemy had proven itself willing to negotiate. Sometimes you're -- the enemy will be willing to write-off their prisoner, particularly if they know that they've got the other side on their last legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, getting back to these types of manoeuvres by guerrilla forces, units, or groups, would tactics such as ambushes be a part of what these types of units or guerrilla groups would do?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly in the defensive position, since they didn't have enough people to defend the whole pocket. Setting up ambushes on key trails, roads, other areas where the enemy might likely try to attack from would be a very appropriate form of warfare. This fits in with the asymmetric warfare concept I talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that asymmetrical warfare also include trying to break what's known as lines of communication of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be in a larger picture. That's not asymmetric; that's actually interdicting the line of communication, which you try to do in any type of warfare. Cut the enemy off from his supplies and make it very difficult for the enemy to receive supplies. And if we're -- area of operations, that's a key part of it is having small raiding parties operating back their tech and convoys, otherwise disrupting the supply of the forward lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the capture of weapons in these types of raids or action be a reasonable tactic of such groups?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. These are questions which are addressed to -- which should be addressed to an expert. If this witness can be asked whether he actually heard about this, or experienced it, or saw it, but at this stage it is simply asking the witness to -- either to speculate or to give what would be an expert opinion about whether such-and-such a tactic would be a reasonable tactic. The question is whether actually he observed that tactic, whether he saw it, whether it was something he learned when he was in the pocket. Otherwise we're in the realms of expert opinion and/or speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I believe correctly, I'll try and pull it forth in the transcript, that Lieutenant Colonel Dudley was asked yesterday in particular about the expertise that he had gained, not as only an airborne officer and intelligence officer, 13 years, I believe, of infantry. We have talked about C3I, command, communication, control, intelligence, without relating it to any particular incident. So I'm just exploring these areas that the Defence sought and thought was relevant to raise on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, that's a different matter, Your Honour. I asked about C3I as to whether that was something which the witness observed, whether in fact those conditions for command and control and communications existed on the ground. As to whether he's served -- whether he's had 13 years of experience, et cetera, it's not an issue of what experience he had. It is a question of what question is put to him. An expert -- a witness can have all sorts of expertise, but unless he is here as an expert witness, then he should be asked factual questions about what he observed, what he heard, what conclusions he drew, not whether absolutely in the abstract a certain tactic would be reasonable -- would be reasonable. All my questions were related to the situation as he observed it in Srebrenica in March 11 to March 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he also testified yesterday about advice, particular advice, that he was giving to the -- the people or the defenders of Srebrenica at the time and tactical defence of Srebrenica and so on and so forth. So at this point in time, unless we really get into technicalities that belong to -- strictly to an expert witness, I would go along, if we come to that stage, obviously I will stop Ms. Sellers. So far I think we are in the perimeters of the same kind of testimony that he gave yesterday and also earlier on today. Okay. Let's -- Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I believe I asked you whether lines of communication would be part of things that units and guerrilla groups were trying to attack. And the next question I want to ask is that would it be, at times, feasible for several groups or units to act in a manner to carry out several types of these type of tactics, a combination of ambush, a combination of breaking lines of communication or getting enemy weapons?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Within the pocket while I was there, these groups would have been able to muster maybe 200 men to do that kind of attack. Can I have a map, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would the witness be handed the same map that he used yesterday 965 or 96 -- 995, 4, or something like that. 996, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Eastern Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Lieutenant Colonel. I would suggest that the technicians focus on the area -- no, no, you need to bring -- focus further up. Start between -- yes, that's about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And focus, possibly, because the words are barely visible here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The Drina River separated Serbia from Bosnia. Along this road were several key bridges that supplied material to the Bosnian Serb forces. There -- because the terrain was so split up, it was very difficult for the Serbs to move off the main hardball roads with supplies. Those roads also were not adequate for trucks, heavy -- other heavy types of equipment. Therefore, one of the key reasons why the Serbs needed to take out the Srebrenica pocket, or at least significantly shrink it, was to deny the enemy access to interdicting their main roads along their lines of communication. You can see also that Srebrenica sat very close to Bratunac and to the key bridges and up further to Zvornik. That made it very -- so pushing the pocket back from the north and the south kept the Muslim forces from being able to get out and interdict those supplies or those main avenues of communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, on the opposite side, those fighting against the restrictions that the Serbs might have been imposing, would it have been a goal to break those bridges so that the Serbs wouldn't be supplied and to break any lines of communication that they would have as a military goal?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this location, one of the key things that I found interesting is that the Muslims did not destroy any bridges and they did not rip up any road, and that was one thing I found very interesting. I suspect the key reason they did not do it was they did not have the high explosives or the engineering capability to rig explosives to rig explosives to destroy these hard targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, talking about the terrain - and you mentioned that in one of your previous answers - what type of terrain favours the use of light artillery versus heavy artillery or tanks?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This terrain handled both -- and I'll talk to each one separately --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "this terrain," are you referring now to the terrain in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrain in Srebrenica where I was operating. If you have a known hard target or a road or someplace else we can have a military observer looking at it, it favours just about any type of indirect weapons fire that you can use. In this case, for instance, when you were at the soccer field, the Serbs were effectively using heavy mortars or heavy artillery. In the more broken-up terrain off the main roads where it was very difficult to see a -- what the enemy was up to, then they would have to shell indiscriminately or engage the enemy with direct-line fire or with some very small mortars because they knew where the enemy was located. Of course, they could not also take their tanks, their artillery, their mortars, off the main roads because the terrain wouldn't support them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the terrain supporting other types, would it be more favourable to other types of military actions? Could you explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to just use this picture here. This terrain all through here had very small trails on it, but it was not capable of supporting heavy artillery or any type of armoured vehicles. Therefore, it was very easy for the light infantry-type forces that were inside Srebrenica, the Muslim forces, to infiltrate in, infiltrate out, do a quick raid, without being interdicted by artillery or other types of indirect fire because the Serbs didn't know where they were and they didn't have the capability of locating them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in that sense would there actually be some advantage of time in terms of the types of tactics for armed persons who knew the terrain, who knew the back woods, persons who were carrying weapons that were lighter than heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, and this was the one advantage that the Muslim defenders did have. I didn't see any other advantages, but, you know, being on foot and lightly armed and infiltrating in and out of the woods give them a distinct advantage over the Serbs, who were set piece in their offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned yesterday something you referred to as dual loyalty, protecting your own homeland, individually your house, your homeland, and being with your force. Is that seen as a type of advantage or is that just merely a factual situation, sir?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you were fighting for your home, you have a lot more reason to fight, and let me refine this even further. Soldiers a lot of times don't fight for nebulous causes, they fight for their buddy, for their small unit, for the honour of the -- and integrity of the group that they are with and for that group's survival. That's where a soldier focusses. And in this type of a conflict, that type of loyalty gets quickly necked down to keeping you and your buddies and your families alive and you really don't care a whole lot about the bigger picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday you mentioned -- you gave a delineation of three types of soldiers: There was the professional soldier, the reservists, and then what you termed the type of citizen soldier?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, could any of these three types of soldiers participate in guerrilla tactics or the asymmetrical tactics you've described?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. If a professional soldier could infiltrate in and take over leadership of a group like that, he would be able to provide them with more military expertise in how to carry out offensive and defensive operations. However, I would like to note I did not see that in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question goes to the following: Would any of those three categories, if you were part of the enemy forces, would each or any of these three categories be considered a soldier in terms of firing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, firstly, already the witness has just answered about what he actually saw in Srebrenica, and it's clear from Ms. Sellers' question she's less interested in what he saw but in speculating about something else. And secondly, in terms of terminology, I object to any question in which basically some categorisation is imposed on this witness. Perhaps he can be asked what he means by soldier. He explained yesterday, if he needs to explain again. But he's gone through this in detail yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day, Ms. Sellers, if he tells you: Yes, I considered them as soldiers, would he have made them soldiers if they were not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be his opinion after he gave forth his explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but this is precisely where Mr. Jones was right earlier on to an extent. I mean, this is where it becomes an expertise because he didn't see this happening in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
