utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll make it more concrete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you consider some of the men that you saw in Srebrenica, the Muslim side, to be that category of citizen soldiers you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer not to use the term soldier on them as military combatant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military combatant. Would you look at them as military combatants as being legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to at this point going go back to your two watchers or maybe as your relationship changed with them you would give -- ascribe to them a different title. Did they become the persons who accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the term assistants, because that is exactly what they did. Is they assisted me in accomplishing my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they go around with you when you visited different parts of the perimeters in order to find out where to make the drops of food?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I either had one or both of them with me. They provided security for my person and they also assisted me in liaising with the local people that I met with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they knowledgeable about the perimeters?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are these perimeters the same thing that one could call the defence lines or the lines between the two sides, the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one way of putting it, yes. I would call it line of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Line of conflict. And you testified yesterday that to your knowledge in Srebrenica that on those lines of conflict there was a rotation of people to maintain the lines?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a formal rotation. One of the things I noticed is that individual groups would go out and individual groups would come back. And there wasn't a lot of cross-fertilisation within the town between these different groups. So there wasn't what I would say a formal rotation per se, but there seemed to be a gentlemen's agreement between these different groups that we will be on for 24, 48, 72 hours and then it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a good military tactic to --

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, please, I do appeal to you to show consideration for the recorders and the interpreters. It is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please try to allow a pause between -- a short pause between question and answer, otherwise we will have problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we just ask when you will be taking a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be taking a break in five minutes' time. That's the result, actually, of -- she is right -- Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just before Ms. Sellers puts a question. Again, I object to the question of saying: Is that a good tactic. And particularly in fact when there is such a rapid answer. It becomes unclear what actually is being referred to. The witness said that he noticed individual groups would go out and come back, a gentlemen's agreement. So if Ms. Sellers is asking whether that is a good military tactic, I again object that it's an expert question. But let's be clear what the "it" refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not an expert question; it's a question of phrasing the question. I agree that as phrased I would accept your objection, but it can be phrased -- you heard about this practice that was being resorted to. Did you agree with it at the time? So -- and at that point in time it's no longer an expert opinion; it becomes a very legitimate question. But I think we need to go back a little bit because we did not have the entirety the witness's answer on the record. Let me try to concentrate on this. Lieutenant Colonel, please follow me and I would ask you to focus on what's missing from your answer. Line 17 on the previous page, page 42. Now are these perimeters the same ones -- the same one could call the defence lines or the sides of warring factions? "A. That is one way I would put it, yes. "Q. Line of conflict. And you testified yesterday that to your knowledge in Srebrenica that on those lines of conflict there was a rotation of people to maintain the lines. "A. I wouldn't call it a formal rotation. One of the things I noticed is that individual groups would go out and individual groups would come back, and there wasn't a lot of cross-fertilisation in town between these two groups. So there wasn't a formal rotation, per se, but there was a gentlemen's agreement that you will be on for 24" -- and I recall hearing you say for 24, 42 -- 48 or 72 hours. And then you come back and I take over. Can you repeat that in your own words so that we integrate that part of your testimony, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I said was I would see one group spend 24, 48, or 72 hours upon the front lines. Then they would come back and change out with another group who would be making their way out to replace them. Because the communications were so poor, it was more of a gentlemen's agreement that we'll be -- spend so much on the front lines then it's your turn. However, I didn't see any official or very coordinated rotation of forces from the front lines that you would see in a professional military environment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we had the objection. And we can follow-up from there. And finish this question and we'll have a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That rotation, whether it was done through a formal or informal way, did that make good military sense to you to always have someone on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Because otherwise the enemy will quickly discover that that area is not defended and use it to initiate offensive operations, particularly if that area is thinly populated with enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a half an hour's break now, and that means we'll resume just past 10.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. You may proceed, Ms. Sellers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I'd like to continue on that same line of questioning. You testified on direct examination the importance of communication, communicating among military combatants, soldiers, or fighters. Could you tell the Trial Chamber that given the terrain in the Srebrenica area, what types of communication would be the most advantageous or merely possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can you -- I think I can imagine what your objection is. Can you rephrase your question, please? Because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just state then -- let me ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, would it be advantageous to use hand-held Motorolas in communicating on terrain within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Motorola radio was designed for short-range communications with line of sight. Therefore, it was very inadequate and inappropriate for military operations in the Srebrenica terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be only appropriate if soldiers or fighters were within range, sight range, of each other, but not necessary hearing range of each other to use this type of apparatus?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Motorola could be used for communications within the same small unit as long as they didn't have a large hill or other physical obstacle that would block the ability of the Motorolas to be a useful communications device. In Srebrenica, I would say it would probably be 500 metres, maybe a thousand metres that the Motorola would be useful in that type of environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the environment in Srebrenica be conducive to placing radio equipment on high altitudes in order to transmit communication?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let's use my specific example. The first night we were in the PTT building and also when we were trying to get into the enclave, we tried to use our tactical satellite communications to get information out. Because of the very narrow mountain valleys, we could not get line of sight with the satellite that we needed to complete the link. Therefore, in Srebrenica communications were difficult at best, and getting to high ground was one of the key requirements for good communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the higher the ground, the better the communications between persons, units, or forces? Would that be correct -- in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily -- yes, let me -- I personally have -- would have an objection to that question as put, but I want to hear what Mr. Jones has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, it's simply that that conclusion which Ms. Sellers is drawing doesn't arise at all from the question -- the answer which has been given, but I think the witness can probably clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because, Ms. Sellers, if you're using an Motorola -- an ordinary Motorola --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I can hear you better now in my cold and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are using a Motorola, an ordinary Motorola, between two persons, two individuals, which -- within the operative distance for the purpose of a Motorola and within sight of each other, it doesn't make a difference whether they are on top of a mountain or whether they are down below in the valley, provided they can communicate with each other and they are -- because they are within range of communicating. So that is why your question, as put, is not acceptable. You need to rephrase it. Let --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I used the term, and this might show my lack of technical expertise in front of the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which I can confirm --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- of radio equipment. And at this point I was not -- I was thinking of other radio equipment where you have airwaves and not Motorola. Excuse me for not being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but then make it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I'm now shifting from Motorolas. I understood what you said about Motorolas needing some type of line of sight or certain other distance. If we were talking about other types of communication equipment, RUPs, there I'm asking would being on higher ground be advantageous to this type of radio communication?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the communications device and the techniques that you're using to communicate with. I'm going to give some specific examples from within the pocket that will help clarify, I think, your question. Motorolas, of course, direct line of sight between one Motorola and another. Large hill, building, et cetera, will interrupt that communications. Each communication device is also limited by its capabilities. A tactical satellite could communicate just about anywhere in the world, as long as we could have a link to the satellite. In Bosnia the UNPROFOR forces were using radios that required to be bounced off the atmosphere and then back down to another location. And atmospherics had a lot to do with their ability to communicate. However, they were the perfect piece of equipment in hilly, rugged terrain because they could bounce off the atmosphere and not through a hill. So it depends on the device you're using on where you can communicate from and how effectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also if I may interrupt you. Also repeaters, or the existence of repeaters would make all the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now tell us in regard to your testimony yesterday about ham radios. I'm just asking about the capacity of communication with ham radios. What type of range do you think could be reached within the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ham radio is not designed for short-range communications; it requires atmospheric balance. And therefore, communicating inside the pocket from one ham radio operator to another would not be very advantageous. The other key problem with using a ham radio, an unsecure ham radio, is the enemy can intercept every single word you utter, therefore, you would have no privacy particularly for military communications. So therefore it was very inadequate for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of problems that could arise by one side hearing the communications of the others, is it advantageous to you to use codes, such as letters or numbers?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two parts to that answer. First off I would try never to use unsecure means of communications in a combat environment, ever, because I don't want the enemy to be able to target my location and therefore maybe drop an artillery round on me or find out where I'm operating, what location I'm operating at. You can intercept other types of communications, but short bursts before the enemy can acquire your location is important for survival. The second part, even using codes and numbers can be intercepted and deciphered. Therefore, you would prefer not to even use codes, if you can help it. But, yes, if I had to work in an unsecure mode, I would have very short bursts and I would use key words and/or numbers to indicate a specific pre-arranged military activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what you've just testified about, the caution that one takes, would changing the radio frequency, if you had to use radio frequency that could be intercepted, would that also be a reasonable means of trying to evade having your messages detected?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely, yes. And more frequently you change them, the harder it is to intercept them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask now about a form of communications that you testified about yesterday, and that's couriers. Would you tell the Trial Chamber what you mean by couriers.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a combat environment where you lack encrypted communications devices or you have a difficulty in communicating because of the terrain, couriers provide a secure means of getting messages from one commander to another commander as long as the people who are sending the messages can put it effectively in writing. The problem with couriers is they can be intercepted and/or killed and they are also very slow, particularly if they are travelling on foot. Therefore, it means for a very slow reaction by friendly forces in support of each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be advantageous with a courier, use of couriers or courier system, that the person be very familiar with the terrain?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He must be because if he gets lost and falls into enemy hands, then he and his message have been compromised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, given certain circumstances, that a courier would transmit oral communication as opposed to a written communication?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. However, fatigue and other combat environments makes for inaccurate transmission of orders, as we saw in earlier centuries of military units. Therefore, I would commit my message in writing whenever possible to make sure that my exact intentions had been communicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And speaking of that, you've mentioned commands. Now, commands are often - and correct me if I'm wrong - given in written form?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And you want to be very specific in your written communications so that there's no question as to what your intent is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a command in a written form, could that be either by handwriting or by writing with a typewriter or any other device --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones -- before you answer, Lieutenant, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, the last 12 questions or so are all completely an abstract discussion on commands and various systems which might exist. I haven't seen a single specific question dealing with anything which this witness observed in Srebrenica. A lot of it anyway is axiomatic as to what might be advantageous and what might not be. I really don't see any questions which are specifically for this witness and within what he's testified about as having seen and observed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we -- I have to uphold Mr. Jones' objection, of course. But on the other hand, why do you ask the witness whether a command in a written form could be either handwritten or by writing with a typewriter or any other -- of course it could be with whatever is available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I don't think -- do you require Lieutenant Colonel Dudley to tell you how a written message could be created?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if Lieutenant Colonel Dudley would like to, yes, but I'm happy to accept the proposition. I can move on. We're still in the realm of communication within this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, what I mean to say, Ms. Sellers, is this: That, yes, of course communication can be handwritten. Yes, of course, it could be typed out. Yes, of course, it could be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Oral?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is if you don't have a typewriter available, you cannot type it out. And if you don't have paper available, you cannot write it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would agree with that proposition, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the essence of the whole thing that we are discussing, basically, in the context of the rest of the evidence that we've had is what was possible at the time and what was actually done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, then we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he could know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because basically I don't know if he is in the position to tell us whether there was any paper available, whether there was any typewriter, were any type writers available or any computers, what type of typewriters, mechanical or electrical ones at the time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask one more absurd question, and I'll move right on to an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If an order is written on a back of a paper that has previously been used, does that in any way diminish the impact of the validity of the order to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specify what was written on it before. Was it crossed out and made sure that that wasn't the piece of communication?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is this witness really being asked to comment on whether an order would be valid if it's written on the back of another piece of paper completely in the abstract without considering which army, what circumstances, what time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I'll move to my next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think we are wasting time on this, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If you'll just allow me one minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's like beauty, Ms. Sellers. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. So Lieutenant Colonel Dudley might give it importance; someone else might not. And say what kind of message this is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. I would now ask that we're going to look at P446. I believe it's going to be brought up on Sanctions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I would ask you to watch your screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We would appreciate if the witness would see the original as well and not just a translation. Actually, I can see the original document -- oh, sorry, it's a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a video, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We weren't seeing it. But that's also for future reference for any of these documents. We want him to see the B/C/S original. I accept this is a video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- on our screen we actually have the name -- a name of a person appearing there, and I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I make it clear that I'm not using the transcript at all. This will be completely visual, and I will not be asking about identification of any people within this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Surely there's a way of showing it without the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I would definitely prefer to have this video shown without the transcript because the transcript doesn't serve only to identifying anyone who may be speaking there, but it also contains other matters. And I don't know what your question is going to be, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, I will be asking about objects, and I would like to say at this point in time it would be rather difficult to remove the transcript. I wonder could I ask the witness to only look at the picture and to please not focus on the transcript. And as I've given assurances to both Defence counsel and Your Honours, there will be no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, do you see in the lower left-corner of this picture what appears to be a typewriter? Would you look closely.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be a typewriter. It could be something else also.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask we move backwards just a tiny bit and go forward again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears to be a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could we continue to roll the film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, do you see on the desk and basically positioned to the middle of this video clip what appears to be either books or papers?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see papers on the desk, and I see a square/rectangular dark brown/black object.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, do you now see what appears to be another array of papers laying on the desk in front of the person?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the person appear to be hand -- holding something in their hand?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appear to be holding a pen or a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, now I'd like to ask some other questions, again related to what you've testified concerning military tactics or guerrilla warfare. Because a group, unit, might be using guerrilla warfare, does that mean that they do not have to plan those actions?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All actions should be planned in advance, particularly contingency actions, because you never know what's going to happen in warfare. The more time you have to plan, the more prepared your forces are to conduct that operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke to your assistants, Senad and Zele, did they ever talk to you about the planning of any of the actions that they went on?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd like to make a specific statement at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to see the command centre so I could coordinate with the key leadership, and I was never able to do that. So I don't know any planning or other military coordination that took place inside the pocket while I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you've spoken about a variety of types of acts, whether they be communications, ambushes, blocking lines of communication, and raids. Now, would all of those types of acts lend themselves to planning operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I simply don't understand the question. "Would they lend themselves to planning operations?" And surely the question is: Were these planned or something. I don't mean -- aren't we interested in this witness's testimony about what he actually experienced and saw in Srebrenica? He's explained: "I don't know any planning or any other military coordination that took place inside the pocket while I was there." And now he's asked this question: "Would these types of acts lend themselves to planning operations?" I simply don't understand what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would have to agree with you, Mr. Jones. The question itself is not clear, Ms. Sellers. I'll read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could I rephrase it, Your Honour, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could these type of acts be planned?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're -- in military operations, there are spontaneous and planned operations. And so when you're planning something like an ambush you try to do it as detailed as possible so you don't get ambushed yourself. Blocking lines of communication is something you can plan or, again, take advantage of a target of opportunity. The same thing with raids. You usually try to plan them, but if you have a target of opportunity, you can conduct them as unplanned operations. From what I saw in the pocket, minimal planning took place based on the exhaustion of the combatants inside the pocket. Were they probably - and this is an assumption, not a fact - trying to conduct some type of military planning? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in terms of conducting military planning, would that be the role -- would that usually be the role of persons in positions of command?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual planning does not take place with the person in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have a staff that you give them your concept of the operation and that you go out and lead, and they stay back and do the planning, they present the plan to you. You either approve it or modify it or disapprove it. That's the normal military operations. However, in the case of the personnel inside the pocket, I've stated many times before, they were untrained military people. Therefore, their planning would be not well-conducted at best, based on their operational experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you still have an objection, Mr. Jones, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's just the questions alternate back and forth between questions about the pocket and then abstract questions. And that was a typical example. The witness had said that in the pocket they were trying to conduct some type of planning. And then Ms. Sellers goes on to ask a question about whether generally leaving Srebrenica aside in the abstract whether the people in command would plan that, and I don't think it's fair -- we're not going to get the best evidence from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has understood this perfectly well. And in fact when he is being asked what appeared to be partly abstract questions, to say the least, he does convert them to what his actual experience on the ground was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take that into consideration. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Not unless we need to correct the transcript, I don't see where I said "leaving Srebrenica aside."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I believe, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, you've understood my question up until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he did, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask the witness to be shown P84, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we'd like him to see the original, just for comparison as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to ask for P84 on page 4 in the English version. It's under the ERN number 02115046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I do want to make sure the witness can see the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't see from here of course. Is he being shown the original? I don't think so. I think that's a photocopy that we have there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does counsel mean the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like him to see the B/C/S. He's been asked questions about handwritten, typing, and all the rest of it, so I think it's only fair that he sees the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can have that problem solved easily if on the -- on Sanction we have on one side the B/C/S version and on the otherwise the corresponding page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has been done in the past.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It has. We do not have -- we have not put this in Sanctions at this time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As long as he can just consult the original as he has done just to see what -- what document we're talking about, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if both documents could be put, at least for a short time, on the ELMO, so that we ourselves can confirm what is being shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe we can do it by ERN number.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Format for me is very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ERN number -- okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I speak to the usher for just one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask Madam Vidovic possibly to look at this issue for us so we won't confuse the Defence witness. And it's just the order of the page and the B/C/S. If the usher could show that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. May I ask a question, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this a Serb intercepted message or is this an original command/staff publication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll certainly not tell you what it is, Lieutenant Colonel, because that's a question that needs to be answered by us later on or decided later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's point of view -- might I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, from the Prosecution's point of view --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object to that because it's in dispute the status of this document. And I don't know if it's -- if that in fact will be the Prosecution giving evidence as to what this document is. If he can just comment on the face of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let her present to him their point of view of what they are facing. And then of course once he has drawn this distinction between a possibly Serb intercepted document and something else, I mean I will give you all the opportunity to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the Prosecution's point of view and I think we've often introduced documents to witnesses saying what appears to be their title on the front page, and I'm doing no more than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If this is a Territorial Defence Municipal Staff of Srebrenica, the memo pad, and for the Territorial Defence officers. And then we have a series of what appears to be minutes to the meetings that the Territorial Defence officers have attended and that someone has noted down. So this is not a Serb intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is a record of a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like that. That's what the Prosecution claims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would draw your attention to the English page 4, and I'm starting at the bottom of page 4. I would just like to read that. There is one part where it says: "Akif, they are not fortified," that's a contested word, "Gornja Rijeka - the bridge. There is one bunker on the Serbian side and three bunkers on the Bosnian side. 50 of my men ... Poloznik 8, Senahid 10. I will set the ambush near the water. Mist does not clear until 1100 [sic] hours. Attack at 1100 hours. That area cannot be held. Do not set fire until everything has been taken out. It takes a full three hours to get to the place where the wounded will be taken over in a vehicle. Move the unit once the goods have been collected. I will take control of the hour -- of the area in one hour." And then: "Send an ultimatum to Serbia not to open fire. Confiscate the collected goods from the smugglers and set up a warehouse." The document goes on, and I am now referring to after the next ERN number 02115047. It says: "Boat crossings will be covered by an anti-aircraft machine-gun. At the end of the operation, destroy the ferry. It would not be good for withdrawal if they stayed in their houses, in the field. There must be a medical technician in this group. A doctor in Jagodnja. Nedret is to work out a schedule." This part continues down and now I'm reading number 5: "There is a way and the area must be kept under control. We have to carry out this operation because of the food. Ahmo has to recognise the coverage of the area." And then number 9 it says: "Communications: The military police must take mobile radio transmitters and walkie-talkies. They must be distributed. The command post is at the anti-aircraft machine-gun site. The password is the same (Bosna-Dzihad)." And then it lists the number of troops with several names. My question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the text be put on the ELMO, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we were told earlier that this will be on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO, Your Honour, it's not on Sanctions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it on the ELMO? Because on the ELMO what I can see is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We would have to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one. And secondly, Madam Vidovic, did you have an objection or a remark to make?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to read as it is written without inventing that "military police" is written where it isn't and that there are means of communication that don't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offer my apologies. That is a misreading and I do not intend to mislead the witness. "Communications" -- in my translation I have: "The military police must take mobile radio transmitters and walkie-talkies. They must be distributed. The command post is at the anti-aircraft machine-gun site. The password is the same (Bosna Dzihad). Number of troops" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the Bosnian it has "VP" and it has "KM," so it doesn't have military police, it doesn't have command post. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you there. But we need to check it. If you're going to put a question to the witness precisely on this part of the document, then we need to know with precision what it says in its original version.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could we have on the ELMO the original version, that particular paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the practice here is that someone reads out and the interpreters translate, unless the interpreters can read it out themselves and translate directly. What I see is that the VP -- V could be superimposed on an O. Then O/C, I don't know, PAM, which we have heard about in the past. That is an anti-aircraft gun. "KM," which I don't know what it is. So if you could -- usually, Madam Vidovic, you would stand up and help us read what you can see and then the interpreters will translate. But of course I cannot force you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would welcome Madam Vidovic to do that. The Prosecution certainly sees on the original it says "VP." I believe that VP has been translated into the two phrases that I used. I certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but I also saw C -- what looks like a V and an O, one on top of the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I wouldn't rush to say it's a VP or an OP. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I think -- the issue I'd like to raise, with all due respect, Your Honour, is that if we just -- if I just included what was written in the document here "VP" and then "KM" would that satisfy the Defence? Because at this point it's -- what does "VP" or "KM" mean? I think that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I would not be happy with that. You know that I always accept that it is written "VP" when it really is. It isn't the case here. What has been described by the Prosecutor was some communication device differently than it is described here. We have already discussed here, but the Prosecutor is simply not trying to incorporate the objections we've already made and agreed on, and we are in a position now to discuss it in front of a witness and agree upon it without the witness, who is the least called upon to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, we are not agreeing on anything. What would OP mean? What would OP mean? Does it -- would it have a meaning, the acronym OP in Bosnian Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could mean many things, like an operations job, Osman Pavlovic, a name, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you, Ms. Sellers, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will let it stand as is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because at this point in time I cannot agree with you that we have VP and not OP here. What I see is what seems to be O for sure, and then either a V or a Y, because it could also be a Y, but I think it would be a little bit strange in that language to have a Y. So I think it's either OP or VP. And then KM, I don't think there should be difficulty in establishing what KM stands for. PAM, also I don't think -- there should not be any difficulty at all. And then "toki-voki" is a version of walkie-talkie, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, since at this point in time I know that we have a list of different acronyms, and I don't necessarily want to discuss this in front of the witness, we might bring this up in a different session, and I don't think that at this point in time the list has been agreed upon between the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And it is a provisional list of which some of the terminology we are speaking on is in. But for questions of expediency, I can say that -- let's say VOP must take the mobile radio transmitters. And we will not in any way say that it says VP, or OP or VOP. I would just like to move on, because I really think that that's not the main issue of the Prosecution at this point, that I would like to point out and be more than willing, if the Defence finds it to be amenable, to withdraw that part of this testimony under number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was taught many years ago actually to decide what I want before I proceed any further. What do you want in relation to -- what do you want from the witness in relation to this part of the text?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to establish whether there were walkie-talkies? Whether there were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only want to establish that it appears that there was planning in terms of communication, in terms of sabotage, in terms of other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then forget about whether it's OP or VP, because at the end of the day we are not discussing with the witness the existence or otherwise of military police or any other thing that could be called OP.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go straight to what you need to obtain or seek to obtain from the witness and we call it a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I would ask you from the parts of this memo pad that I've just read, is this in line with the type of planning one would do for actions that included ambush, sabotage, and communications?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a few minutes, Your Honour, to actually study the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while the witness is reading I just wish to say that this English translation here reads in a different way. It simply says something that does not feature in the original. It doesn't even say "extension military police." It simply says "military police." And that's the -- our general problem with the use of this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's not jump the gun. I mean, I fully understand the point that you have raised that permeates this and other documents, but let's wait for the witness reaction to the question that was put to him. We have a general question or a question of a general -- generic nature other than a specific one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've read the document and understand it and in as best as it was translated. I would now request that the Prosecution restate their question and let me switch so I can see it in writing, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understood him, he wants to go on transcript mode? Is he in transcript mode? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the question here, it's still on my transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I said: "Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I would ask you from the parts of this memo pad that I've just read, is this in line with the type of planning one would do for actions that would included ambush, sabotage, and communications?" And I mean in terms of what you described as guerrilla tactics.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would -- if it was an operations order, it would be very poorly written. It sounds more like a discussion, and it looks like an intercepted discussion. I would say that this was designed to be a small-level unit raid. And one of the key notes that I have here is that they have moved from a discussion to a list of possible troops to participate in the operation. And if it is a discussion and it was intercepted - and this appears to be intercepted - then they were using non-secure means, which is very sloppy for military operations. Those are my conclusions from looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if this were not intercepted, does that change your opinion of what it said, sir?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like it's going to be a small-unit raid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask Lieutenant Colonel Dudley to turn to what is page 26 in the English version of the document. Again, I think you might want to put the B/C/S on the ELMO. And, Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, yesterday you testified to questions of morale that were important with all troops. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that morale during wartime is something that had to be maintained in order to keep your fighting forces efficient as possible?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would use the term "effective."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did state that probably one of more demoralising things that you witnessed in Srebrenica was the war hospital, that might have been bad for troop morale?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if commanders had to send -- were obligated to have their troops go to that hospital, would one of the ways of lifting the morale be to at least consistently visit any of your troops that had been wounded in actions at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as times allowed, yes. A commander thanking his troops for its service and the troops understanding that the commander is concerned about their health and welfare, yes, that's an important concept of morale. The other key thing is that if the commander is suffering the same deprivations as his troops, that is also a key component to good morale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could I add that would probably be a key component to good -- being a good commander and an effective commander?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily effective, but what I would call a good commander. Let me rephrase that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good commander, whether experienced or not, takes care of his men. That doesn't mean that he understands all the military requirements of a commander, but he is being a good leader by caring about the welfare of his men who serve under him or with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now turn your attention to page 26, and in the English version, sir, I believe it's on the ELMO now, under number 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. -- what's the corresponding page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The ERN in B/C/S, Your Honour -- ERN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see it 02115077 [Realtime transcript read in error "021155"]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct? Okay. So can we have it on the ELMO as well at least for a short while? Yeah. No, no, it's 02115077. Yeah, it's wrong on the -- yeah, on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's 75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's right before it comes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 76. It would be at the bottom of that page. Your Honour, might I continue to read in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it's 5076 that we need to look at from the B/C/S approach?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Page 26 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I'm looking under the number 3 where it says --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you might want to follow along if you can in the English version where it says - and, sir, you might want to follow along if you can in the English version - where it says: "Military activities."

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Number 3: Military activities," I am following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. "Operations have stopped. "The failure of Bedem has completely thrown us off track. We must not allow failure in one operation to affect us so much. "This is also a warning that from now on, the leaders must not be direct participants as well. "In our situation, we must have strategic goals whose achievement is necessary for our survival. Haphazard planning and conduct of operations leads only to the exhaustion of our capacities without any effect. (What is the value of free territory if we are besieged?) "Morale and the political situation in units. "The relationships between commanders, personnel, and the staff." My question to you, after reading that part: Even when undertaking small unit raids or guerrilla warfare, does this reflect the type of concern that leaders and commanders have to have for morale, particularly after an operation is not successful?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to qualify that question. This looks like an after-action review of an operation that went bad. Bedem, to me, looks like the code name for that operation. Yes, these concerns that are expressed could be the concerns of any commander or leadership group concerned about keeping their organisation together after a bad operation, particularly when they have very limited resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to continue now -- I'm still on page 26 in the English, and I'll be going over to page 27. And if you could follow along at the end of page 26 we see that we have now the minutes of the Srebrenica OS staff meeting held on the 22nd of November, 1992, and under Roman numeral I it says: "The failure of the Bedem operation has had a negative impact on us. But we must continue to plan and carry out operations. We should attack Kunjerac and Radijevici for food. This would not have to be a big operation but a small one. The same applies to Cosici. "Radijevici-Bjelovac (Kunjerac), carry out the operation simultaneously. "Ramiz: A unit consisting of 50 to 70 men should be formed for these small operations. "Naser: The situation in Glogova has been reconnoitred, and the operations there should be carried out simultaneously with Kunjerac (Bjelovac). "Hamed: I agree with Ramiz. "Suljo: I support Hamed and Ramiz. "Zijad to reconnoitre Radijevici. "Ahmo and Sakib to reconnoitre Cosici. "Mido to reconnoitre Bjelovac. "Glogova has been reconnoitred. "Naser undertakes to form an elite platoon. "Hazim will reconnoitre Voljevica. "Sabotage the bus before the above operations. "Continue activity. "Sabotage operations to continue simultaneously." Now, my question to you is that from what I've just read, would that be in line with continuing types of guerrilla military tactics after a defeat and the proper planning of such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's just -- we are purely in the realm of what would be expert testimony here. These are events from November 1992. The witness isn't being asked anything about what he knew in the pocket at all, and if it's the case that we can simply go through every single document which has been introduced as exhibits and put in front of the witness as an expert and say does this show that, does this show the other, and the witness is being used for a purpose entirely different from what -- from why he was brought here. This exercise that Ms. Sellers is conducting can be conducted with absolutely any document in the trial because he's not being asked about his own knowledge, about his own experience, whether he knows anything about these events. He's simply being put propositions, hypotheticals, what conclusions would he draw. I agree if an expert were here who was giving evidence -- that would be one thing. And if the Prosecution's position answer is, well, he has expertise, that's not an answer. He is not an expert witness. I have to insist on that. Because if he is, it's entirely a different exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, I believe on direct examination this witness was led to testify that he gave advice to the groups that were in the Srebrenica pocket. He was giving advice to them concerning the front lines in terms of the parameters [sic]. And we briefly went over that today. And he heard about the different types of actions they would undertake for raids. I'm merely relating some of the information or evidence that we have concerning actions and asking him as someone who was giving advice to them: What would this mean? Does it fit into this framework of advice that he had been giving before. I think that's entirely appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Certainly the witness can be asked about the advice he gave; he's spoken about that. But if the Prosecution wants to cross-examine about the advice he gave in March 1993, certainly I have no objection to that. And if he's asked whether he knows about these raids which were referred to here, again that's a matter -- and if the Prosecution were interested in this witness's knowledge they would ask him first of all: Do you know anything about these events on 22 November 1992. Do you know anything about Kunjerac, Bjelovac, Radijevici? It's precisely that he doesn't know anything about that those questions are not being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Basically, Ms. Sellers, Mr. Jones, we -- the way we see it, we are travelling on a very tight rope here and the line of demarcation between expert -- what would be expert testimony and ordinary testimony has become so fine that we do need to draw a line somewhere. Your question borders precisely on this and tends to fall more on the expert side, expert testimony side, than not, although not completely. So what we suggest is that you rephrase your question and ask the witness whether what he has read here corresponds with what he came to know when he arrived in Srebrenica on his -- the intelligence that he had of the events prior to his arrival, because we're talking of October, November here of the previous year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour. I guess that Defence and Prosecution can appreciate what it means to be on the front line right now and back to the witness's hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we have read in this previous section in relationship to Judge Agius' question, how does this correspond to the intelligence that you had concerning the planning, communications, intelligence, and morale of the troops, the Muslim troops in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- one moment, Ms. Sellers, because I recognise Mr. Clifton Johnson on his feet. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Ms. Sellers, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, I believe that you've been asked several times now that the question will be: From what we've just read to compare that to your assessment, your knowledge at the time period you were in Srebrenica as to how this would compare to planning, communications, information that you had.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Before I go further, looking at one small snippet of information does not allow me to grasp a big picture of a military capability. I would want to see several days of transcripts and a map of the operational area and the approximate forces participating on both sides so that I could do a decent analysis. This does not give me enough information that I need to say yes or no as to those capabilities. I will go back to Srebrenica when I was there 11 through 28 March, 1993. Looking at the capability of the fighters on the ground at that time, they were not capable of well-coordinated operations, particularly conducting multiple raids at multiple locations in coordination with each other. They were too exhausted and too ill-equipped to be effective against the Serb forces in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And from what we have read out in my past several questions, does that appear to you to contrast, this undertaking of different raids, contrast with the forces or soldiers that you saw in the time period when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I hardly think it's fair to the witness. He's just said that a snippet doesn't enable him to comment, that he would need to see several days of transcripts in the operational area and approximate forces, and he's been asked again still to do that. And he's said that he doesn't -- [cannot distinguish between speakers because of overlap] -- I don't see why he should be forced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already answered this question, and I mean he attributes in his mind the incapacity of the ground forces that he knew of to carry out raids because of the fatigue and whatever else, because I don't want to use words that he may not have used. But I think we have the answer to that question already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the time period. I was asking for a contrast, and it appears to me that the witness would want to have several other portions read out to him, which I -- for periods of time for the cross-examination would be rather difficult, but I think he's saying that he would need more information prior to making the assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just want to make clear. Is the witness be aware that the question was not comparing the situation which you got to know in March and with the actual situation at that time, but to compare March 1993 with the alleged events which took -- have -- has been reported about and that -- in November of 1992? You are aware of this difference of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking -- yes, Your Honour. Looking at the top of the transcript, I was able to figure out -- we were talking about November 1992, because that was the date on the transcript. My concern here is I am familiar with many different types of military operations to include disinformation operations, and I would like to know how this was communicated. Was it intercepted? Was it written as part of a meeting? Who was it intended for? I've got to get some more details before I can make an honest assessment of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Lieutenant Colonel. I think you have -- you have this problem and you have to live with it, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will not be able to assist the witness in this matter. I would, then, like to move on to some other documents. I would ask that the witness could be shown P3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, you have before you a document that is dated Srebrenica, the 18th of October, 1992, confidential. And then under number 2 it says: "I order to establish in full by the 25th of October constant communications by couriers and communications met from lower units to higher units and suggest in accordance with the military organisation and establishment structure, as defined by order number 2892." My question to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can he be shown the original. That was my request at the outset, for all of these he sees the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Jones. I think we have that request, and I see the witness indicating to me that he has it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the original in B/C/S? I believe that's what the Defence counsel wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, my question to you in particular for paragraph number 2 is that in terms of the Srebrenica enclave, was the establishment of a communications by courier something that would be favourable to the terrain according to your experience in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to -- have to go back and restate a few things and then I'll answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, C3I, or command, control, communications, and intelligence, are all vital parts of good effective command and control on the ground for a commander. If you lack one or more of these areas, then you will not be able to effectively control your command. In Srebrenica, lacking adequate communications devices to send and receive reports and orders, particularly on broken terrain, a courier system would have to be established in order to conduct any type of effective communications between a commander and his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask if this document can be taken away and we show the witness P7, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, we'll have a break in about -- between five and ten minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make your own calculations when it's more convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to look at this document. It's one from Srebrenica, 31st of October, 1992. It has "order" written about one-third down the page. And it says: "All units of the Srebrenica armed forces will bear numerical codes as follows." And then I'll draw your attention down to number 9. It says: "Srebrenica Independent Battalion, 7510." And then the last paragraph in this order says: "A numerical code of the battalions within the brigade shall be determined by adding number 1, 2, or 3 to the numerical code of the brigade." And my question to you, sir, giving codes to different segments or units of an army, is that advantageous in terms of communications among groups within the military structure, from your experience in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With any type of encryption using an alphanumeric code makes for clear communications in a military environment. Either secure or unsecure, a sequence of alphanumeric numbers would make for a quick and efficient communications between units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would now ask for Lieutenant Colonel Dudley to be -- have this document withdrawn and to be shown P10, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while that document is being given to you, I want to ask you: Were you aware during your time period in Srebrenica of a communications centre, a military communications centre, in a place called Lovak [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to look at P10. It's a document dated the 20th of October, 1992, from Srebrenica. It's an order -- it says: "For the members of the armed forces of Srebrenica, those are as follows." And it list 22 persons. And the bottom of the page it says: "The pass allows the above members to stay in and travel from Srebrenica to Tuzla and back." From your experience in Srebrenica and during wartime, is that part of a function of leaders or commanders to authorise passes, whether they be individual, group passes, to persons who are members of the military?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Define "pass" for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did he say? Yeah. Okay. Can we see the top of the -- because when you read out the document, I don't think you read out group -- that it is a group pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's number one. And secondly, there is included in this document also what appears to be a kind of weapon that these persons will be carrying. That's number two. It's another distinctive quality in -- And, Mr. Jones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, we're drifting back into the realms of expert evidence. The first part of the question makes it sound like it's a factual question: From your experience in Srebrenica. I then expected the question to be: Are you familiar with passes being authorised for people to travel back and forth from Srebrenica and Tuzla. But then it shifts into an abstract question. And it's not fair to the witness. Is he being asked about Srebrenica, what he experienced, or is he being asked about an expert witness question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree a hundred per cent. I think you need to more or less approach the matter as suggested by Mr. Jones. And since the witness also is not comfortable with the word -- the generic word "pass," I think you need to put him in the picture exactly what you mean by "pass." And I'm asking this -- I'm saying this because, as I said, the -- there is also an indication of the weapon they are supposed to be carrying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that justifies hundred per cent the witness's request to have the nature of this pass that you are referring to from this document clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: If I go first to the question of the pass and then I'll be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- address the questions raised in the objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the top of the document it does say "group pass." At the bottom of the document it says: "Pass allows the above members to stay in and travel from Srebrenica to Tuzla and back." Now, when you were in Srebrenica, you testified that one of your watchers, assistants, came from Tuzla to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether he had permission to come to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he told me was that he was a volunteer of a small group of lightly armed men who infiltrated from Tuzla to Srebrenica. How they organised that group and what certifications they provided to that group I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar under military structures with permission given to members of groups to go from one place to another, authorised permission?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That takes many different variants. A pass in my terminology means that you have a leave coming to you, and therefore you can be absent from your unit for a specific period of time for rest and recreation. Another type of pass would be provided to either a civilian or a convoy of vehicles to pass from one military location to another, given the permission to travel on a specific road if questioned. The third type of pass would be a document that somebody would carry with them that would allow them to show permission to travel as an individual between different locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if one were to look at your different considerations, and particularly the last one, is it from your understanding that when you have a pass that permits you to travel from one location to the other during times of war, and particularly as in Srebrenica, that persons could carry -- could travel with weapons?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. What this is telling me is this was an armed group who is not known to everybody on both sides of the line, and therefore this was certifying them as official BiH fighters and therefore they were to be accepted into the other enclave or location as certified Bosniaks versus BSA members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, maybe you can help us or maybe you can't, sir, if you notice after the names of the person what appears to be the rifle, there is a number. Now, from your experience in Srebrenica, does that number tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number tells me nothing. All it means is that they have assigned a specific number to a specific person for whatever reason. They usually only issue one number to one person to keep it clear so you don't have confusion. Otherwise, I have no any idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and his experience in Srebrenica, I don't see how it could help him to understand, especially if you look at number 22. M, whatever that means, 56, and then 348, 53-C. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not hesitate to offer what it means. At this time I would be more than willing to take the break, as Your Honour suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. We'll have a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How much longer do you think you require the witness, Ms. Sellers? Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I've informed the Defence that I hope to conclude by 1.00, five after, and there should be adequate time, if we're going until quarter of 2.00 today for cross or re-cross or re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Are you going to start with the next witness today or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, tomorrow. And as I said, I've spoken to Mr. Wubben about that witness, and I'm going to try and stick actually to an hour and a half, and so it might be possible to finish with him tomorrow as well. But of course there's no -- that's a matter between us, just to let you know that that's what we're endeavouring to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We would appreciate if you reach an agreement on that, because we would take advantage from it. So, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask right now if the witness could recall his testimony -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Dudley, you testified yesterday that at times there was sirens that would go off in Srebrenica while you were there and that that would be a signal for some form of mobilisation. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: REX EDWARD DUDLEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. As I recall, that siren would be used to signify either incoming aircraft or occasionally to mobilise forces. And that's all I remember about the siren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
